why: The collect verdict and status vocabulary has THREE implementations of one rule
set: internal/herd/collect (a local herdr worktree), internal/cloud/collect (a
remote branch, read from the laptop) and cloud/factory/src/worker-collect.ts (the
same remote, read from the Worker through GitHub's API).
The first two were the SAME TYPE by import until epic 3j4 stopped the cloud path
importing ticks internals, so drift between them was impossible by construction.
They are now copies. The failure mode that creates is silent and it INVERTS A
VERDICT: re-spell `NEEDS_CONTEXT` or `ready-to-merge` in one place and a cloud run
and a herd run disagree about what happened to the same tick, with nothing failing
anywhere — the report just quietly means something different.
So all three read this file, and a one-sided edit fails a build.
MORE THAN THE CONSTANTS. The status line REGEXP is part of the contract, and a
fixture that pinned only the four status words would miss both of its traps:
1. `DONE_WITH_CONCERNS` must precede `DONE` in the alternation. Under the wrong
order `STATUS: DONE_WITH_CONCERNS` parses as `DONE` — a verdict inversion, on
the exact status a human most needs to see. Today that is defended TWICE: by
the order, and by the `\b` after the capture group (`_` is a word character,
so `DONE\b` cannot match inside `DONE_WITH_CONCERNS`). Because the two
defences overlap, NO input distinguishes a re-ordered alternation on its own —
which is exactly why `status_line_pattern` below pins the pattern text
byte-for-byte, ordering included. Re-order it and all three builds go red even
though behaviour has not changed yet. The `done_with_concerns_*` parse cases
then catch the other half: they fail the moment the `\b` guard is weakened,
which is what makes a re-ordering dangerous.
2. The markdown `decoration` trim set. Workers write prose, and a status line
inside a bullet or bolded is still a status line — but a set that grows or
shrinks on one side only makes two implementations disagree about whether a
report has a status at all, which is the `missing-result` verdict.
READERS (all three must stay in this list):
- internal/herd/collect/contract_test.go
- internal/cloud/collect/contract_test.go
- cloud/factory/test/collect-vocabulary.test.ts
The four verdicts, in the order the checks run: the first failing check wins.
All three implementations define all four, spelled exactly like this.
`unknown` means the durable evidence could not be READ — an unreachable remote,
a rate-limited API, a base commit this checkout does not have. It is never a
verdict ON the worker. Only the two implementations that read a REMOTE can fail
this way, so internal/herd/collect deliberately does not define it and its
contract test asserts that absence rather than ignoring it.
The four statuses a worker's report may end with. Independent of the verdict:
a worker can commit, write a report and still report BLOCKED.
The two statuses that are an escalation regardless of verdict — what
Report.NeedsHuman / needsHuman() flag. Dropping one here silently stops a human
being told.
The regexp source, byte-for-byte. Go's `regexp.MustCompile(...).String()` and
JavaScript's `RegExp.prototype.source` both return the pattern text, and the
syntax used here is common to both, so one string pins all three.
This is what makes the DONE_WITH_CONCERNS-before-DONE ALTERNATION ORDER
enforceable at all — see `why` at the top of this file. Any edit to the pattern
in any one implementation fails three builds; if the edit is intended, change it
here and confirm the parse cases below still describe what you meant.
The markdown a report line may be wrapped in, trimmed from both ends of the line
AND from both ends of the detail. Go holds it as a `strings.Trim` cutset; the
Worker holds it as a character class. The two cannot be compared as text, so it
is pinned BEHAVIOURALLY from both sides: every character in `trimmed` must be
stripped, and every character in `not_trimmed` must NOT be — a set that quietly
grows fails just as loudly as one that shrinks.
INPUT LINE -> PARSED STATUS. `body` is the report text; `status`, `detail` and
`line` are what all three implementations' status parser must return for it.
An empty `status` means the report carries no recognisable status — which is the
`missing-result` verdict, so a case that stops matching is a verdict change too.

cases.name: done_with_concerns_with_detail
why: THE MOST VALUABLE CASE IN THIS FILE. Under a weakened status regexp —
specifically a `DONE`-first alternation that has also lost its `\b` guard —
this parses as status `DONE` with detail `_WITH_CONCERNS — the suite passes
...`, and the report silently means the opposite of what the worker wrote.
It is the exact status a human most needs to see.
cases.body: STATUS: DONE_WITH_CONCERNS — the suite passes but the migration is untested
cases.detail: the suite passes but the migration is untested
cases.line: STATUS: DONE_WITH_CONCERNS — the suite passes but the migration is untested

cases.name: done_with_concerns_bare
cases.why: The same inversion with no detail to hide behind: the status word is the whole payload.

cases.name: done_with_concerns_in_a_blockquote_with_crlf
cases.why: The inversion again through the decoration trim and a CRLF report, which is how a Windows-authored report arrives.

cases.name: a status word with a suffix is not a status
cases.why: The `\b` guard, from the other side. Without it `DONEISH` parses as DONE.

cases.name: NEEDS_CONTEXT with a colon separator
cases.why: The status a cloud run and a herd run must agree means the same thing, with the colon form of the separator.
cases.body: STATUS: NEEDS_CONTEXT: which remote owns the branch
cases.line: STATUS: NEEDS_CONTEXT: which remote owns the branch

cases.name: BLOCKED inside a bolded bullet
cases.why: Workers write prose. A status line in a bullet, bolded, is still a status line — and BLOCKED is an escalation, so failing to see it strands a human.
cases.body:
Some prose first.

- **STATUS: BLOCKED — no credentials for the remote**
cases.line: STATUS: BLOCKED — no credentials for the remote

cases.name: a hash-decorated heading
cases.why: `#` is in the trim set: a report that makes its status a heading still has a status.

cases.name: tab separator with a hyphen
cases.why: Tabs are in both the trim set and the inline whitespace class; the hyphen is a separator, not part of the detail.
cases.body: STATUS:	DONE_WITH_CONCERNS	- flaky test on rerun
cases.line: STATUS:	DONE_WITH_CONCERNS	- flaky test on rerun

cases.name: an en-dash separator
cases.why: The separator class carries all three dashes. Agents emit whichever their prose style produced.

cases.name: the FINAL status line wins
why: The contract is the LAST status line, because a report may quote the
template's four options above its own answer. If an implementation took the
first instead, this report would be read as NEEDS_CONTEXT — an escalation
the worker withdrew.
cases.body:
Report as one of DONE, DONE_WITH_CONCERNS, NEEDS_CONTEXT, BLOCKED.

STATUS: NEEDS_CONTEXT — I thought I was stuck here

Then I found the answer.

STATUS: DONE_WITH_CONCERNS — the last word is the one that counts
cases.detail: the last word is the one that counts
cases.line: STATUS: DONE_WITH_CONCERNS — the last word is the one that counts

cases.name: a decoration character outside the trim set
cases.why: The trim set pinned from the other side: `~` is not markdown decoration, so this line does not begin with STATUS: and is not a status line.

cases.name: a status word that is not one of the four
cases.why: The vocabulary is closed. `SUCCESS` is not a status, and a report carrying only that has no status — the `missing-result` verdict.

cases.name: no status line at all
cases.why: A report that never says. Every field empty, and the verdict that follows is missing-result.
cases.body: The work is done and the branch is pushed.

cases.name: an empty report
cases.why: The degenerate input, pinned so no implementation crashes or invents a status for it.
